Before you visit

Accuracy. A pin marked LOW is the centre of a search area, not an exact spot. Respect. The cemeteries, camps and memorials in this guide are places of remembrance and mourning first: dress and behave accordingly, and many battlefields are private land — view from the road. Travel. Check government travel advice before you plan: the UK and others currently advise against all travel to Russia and Belarus. Safety. Never pick up old ammunition — leave it and call 112.

Remember · Explore · Respect

Briefing

War room briefing · read before moving out

This guide covers the Second World War in Europe from the first shots at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939 to the German surrender signed at Reims on 7 May and in Berlin on 8 May 1945. It is not one battlefield but a whole continent: 160 places in 15 areas, from Liverpool to Volgograd and from Narvik to Malta, chosen so that together they tell the story of how the war began, turned and ended — and what it did to the people caught in it. Two sets of positions are kept apart on purpose:

TIMELINE — 65 historical positions in date order: what happened, where and when, and who was there. TOUR — driving stops in road order, in ready-made routes from one to fifty-two days, or only the area you choose, or your own list. Every stop opens directly in Google Maps.

The accuracy rule

A GPS coordinate can locate a museum, cemetery, bridge or memorial precisely; it cannot turn a battle across a whole city or a forest into an exact point. When the records only place a unit "somewhere in the woods", this guide says so rather than invent a spot, and where historians disagree — over numbers, times or motives — the text tells you. Each position carries a coloured label:

HIGHexact spot known — a landmark, museum, cemetery, memorial, bridge or building, or a position fixed by the recordsMEDIUMwell supported, but the exact spot is uncertainLOWgeneral area only — the pin is the centre of a search area

Words to know

WehrmachtGermany's armed forces as a whole from 1935: the army (Heer), navy (Kriegsmarine) and air force (Luftwaffe)OKW / OKHThe High Command of the Armed Forces and the High Command of the Army; from late 1941 Hitler commanded the army himselfWaffen-SSThe armed branch of Himmler's SS, which grew from a few regiments to some 38 divisions; it fought alongside the army and committed many massacresSS and SDHimmler's Party organisation, which ran the police, the concentration camps and the security service (SD)RSHAReich Security Main Office, under Heydrich and then Kaltenbrunner — the headquarters of the Gestapo, the criminal police and the SDEinsatzgruppenSS and police mobile killing units that followed the army into Poland and the Soviet Union and shot Jews, communists and othersFinal SolutionThe Nazi term for the murder of all of Europe's JewsOperation ReinhardThe 1942–43 programme to murder the Jews of occupied Poland in the camps of Bełżec, Sobibór and TreblinkaLuftwaffeThe German air forceKriegsmarineThe German navy; its U-boat arm was led by Admiral Karl DönitzBlitzkrieg'Lightning war' — fast, concentrated attacks by tanks and aircraft; a label used more by journalists than by German doctrinePanzerGerman tank, and the armoured divisions built round tanksKessel'Cauldron' — a pocket of encircled troopsAtlantic WallThe German coastal defences from Norway to the Spanish border, strengthened under Rommel in 1944West WallGermany's border fortifications, called the Siegfried Line by the AlliesOrganisation TodtThe German construction organisation that built the Atlantic Wall and U-boat bases, largely with forced labourRed ArmyThe Soviet army; its army groups were called FrontsNKVDThe Soviet secret police, responsible for Katyn, deportations and the post-war special campsGreat Patriotic WarThe Russian name for the war against Germany, 1941–45Home Army (AK)Poland's underground army, loyal to the government-in-exile in LondonFFIFrench Forces of the Interior, the armed Resistance in 1944SOESpecial Operations Executive — the British organisation that ran sabotage and agents in occupied EuropeRAF Fighter CommandThe RAF's fighter organisation, which fought the Battle of Britain through its Groups; No. 11 Group defended the south-eastBomber CommandThe RAF's bomber force, under Sir Arthur Harris from February 1942; it bombed mainly by nightEighth Air ForceThe US strategic bomber force in Britain, which bombed by dayEnigmaThe German cipher machine used by all the armed forcesUltraThe British name for intelligence from broken high-level German codes and ciphersLend-LeaseThe US programme, from March 1941, that supplied Britain, the Soviet Union and other Allies with arms, vehicles, fuel and foodBEFBritish Expeditionary Force — the British army in France in 1939–40SHAEFSupreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force, Eisenhower's command in north-west Europe from 194421st Army GroupMontgomery's British and Canadian command in north-west Europe, 1944–45Overlord / NeptuneThe invasion of Normandy; Neptune was its naval and landing phaseBarbarossaThe German invasion of the Soviet Union, 22 June 1941BagrationThe Soviet offensive in Belarus, June–August 1944Market GardenThe airborne and ground attack towards Arnhem, September 1944V-1 / V-2German 'vengeance weapons': a pulse-jet flying bomb and a ballistic rocketCWGCCommonwealth War Graves CommissionABMCAmerican Battle Monuments CommissionVolksbundThe German War Graves Commission (Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge)
Respect the ground. Many places in this guide are cemeteries, camps and execution sites where millions of people are mourned. They are places of remembrance first and tour stops second: dress and behave accordingly, follow the memorials' own rules on photography, and remember that guides at the camps are often descendants of victims or survivors. On the old battlefields, shells, grenades and mines still surface every year: never touch or pick up a metal object — leave it, mark the spot in your mind and call 112. Many positions are on private land: view them from roads and marked paths.

The story in brief

Poland.. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and two days later Britain and France declared war. The Polish army fought hard, but it was outnumbered, attacked from three sides and, from 17 September, stabbed in the back by the Soviet Union under the secret terms of the Nazi–Soviet Pact. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September and the last Polish forces on 6 October. The country was divided between two dictatorships. The Germans set out to destroy the Polish elite and to crowd Poland's Jews into ghettos; in the east, the Soviets deported hundreds of thousands and in 1940 shot some 22,000 Polish prisoners at Katyn and other sites.

The fall of France.. After a winter of 'Phoney War', Germany seized Denmark and Norway in April 1940. On 10 May it attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France. The British and French moved their best armies into Belgium, but the main German blow came through the Ardennes: on 13 May the panzers crossed the Meuse at Sedan and in a week reached the Channel, trapping the northern armies. Some 338,000 men were evacuated from Dunkirk, but France was beaten. It signed an armistice at Compiègne on 22 June, and the Vichy regime under Pétain collaborated with the occupier.

Britain alone.. Churchill refused to negotiate. In the summer of 1940 the Luftwaffe tried to win control of the air over southern England as a prelude to invasion and failed against the RAF's radar-directed fighters; on 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion. The Blitz on British cities went on until May 1941. In the Atlantic the U-boats attacked the convoys that kept Britain alive, while Italy's entry into the war opened fronts in North Africa and the Mediterranean. Germany rescued its ally by conquering Yugoslavia and Greece in April 1941 and Crete in May, and sent Rommel to Libya.

Barbarossa.. On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million men. The Red Army lost millions killed and captured in vast encirclements, and by the autumn the Germans were outside Leningrad and Moscow. Behind them the Einsatzgruppen shot Jewish communities by the tens of thousands, as at Babi Yar in September. But the Soviet state did not collapse. Its factories were moved east, its reserves were thrown in, and on 5 December Zhukov counter-attacked before Moscow. Two days later Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and on 11 December Hitler declared war on the United States.

The Holocaust.. At Wannsee in January 1942 senior officials coordinated the deportation and murder of all Europe's Jews. Death camps were built in occupied Poland — Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka, then Auschwitz-Birkenau and Majdanek — and trains came to them from France, the Netherlands, Greece, Italy, Hungary and everywhere German power reached. In 1942 alone some 2.7 million Jews were killed. By 1945 about six million had been murdered, along with Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, disabled people and others. In the Warsaw ghetto in 1943, and at Treblinka and Sobibór, Jews rose against their killers.

The turning points.. In 1942 Germany struck again in the East, towards the Caucasus oilfields and the Volga. At Stalingrad the Sixth Army was drawn into a street battle, and in November the Red Army encircled it; Paulus surrendered at the start of February 1943. In North Africa the British won at El Alamein in November 1942 and Anglo-American forces landed in Morocco and Algeria; the Axis armies in Tunisia surrendered in May 1943. That same month the escorts beat the U-boats in the Atlantic. In July Germany's last great offensive in the East, at Kursk, failed within a week.

The squeeze.. From mid-1943 Germany was on the defensive everywhere. The Allies landed in Sicily in July and in Italy in September; Mussolini fell and Italy changed sides, but the Germans held most of the peninsula and fought the Allies to a standstill at Monte Cassino until May 1944. The British and American bomber offensive burned Hamburg in July 1943 and in early 1944 destroyed the Luftwaffe's fighter force. In the East the Red Army advanced across Ukraine and in January 1944 ended the siege of Leningrad. Across occupied Europe resistance grew, and so did German reprisals.

Summer 1944.. On 6 June 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy. For ten weeks they fought a bitter battle in the hedgerows and around Caen, until the Americans broke out in late July and two German armies were nearly trapped in the Falaise pocket. Paris was freed on 25 August. In the East, Operation Bagration destroyed Army Group Centre in Belarus from 22 June, and the Red Army reached the Vistula. On 20 July Stauffenberg's bomb failed to kill Hitler. On 1 August the Polish Home Army rose in Warsaw; the Soviets halted across the river, and after 63 days the Rising was crushed.

Autumn and winter.. The Allied pursuit ran out of fuel at the German frontier. Market Garden, the airborne gamble to cross the Rhine at Arnhem in September, failed. Through the autumn the Americans fought slow, costly battles at Aachen and in the Hürtgen Forest. In the Balkans, Romania and Bulgaria changed sides and the Germans left Greece. On 16 December Hitler threw his last reserves into the Ardennes. The Battle of the Bulge took the Americans by surprise, but Bastogne held, and by January the German army had lost the strength it could no longer replace.

The fall of Germany.. In January 1945 the Red Army swept from the Vistula to the Oder, freeing Auschwitz on 27 January. In the west the Allies cleared the Rhineland, crossed the Rhine at Remagen on 7 March and in strength on 23–24 March, and encircled the Ruhr. As they advanced, they found the camps — Buchenwald, Belsen, Dachau — and the world saw what had been done. On 16 April the Soviets attacked towards Berlin; on 25 April Americans and Soviets met on the Elbe. Hitler killed himself on 30 April. Germany surrendered unconditionally at Reims on 7 May and at Karlshorst late on 8 May.

Why the whole route

No one place explains the Second World War in Europe. Westerplatte and Sedan show how fast Germany won in 1939–40; Uxbridge, Bletchley and the Western Approaches bunker show how Britain held on. The cemeteries of Normandy and the memorials of Stalingrad and Prokhorovka show where the war was decided and at what cost. The camps — Treblinka, Auschwitz, Dachau, Belsen — and villages such as Lidice and Oradour show what the war was for in Nazi eyes, and what victory stopped. Seen together, from Gdańsk to Karlshorst, the places add up to one war: a war of armies, industry and codes, and of genocide.

Using your location

Tap the 📍 button at the top right and allow location when your phone asks. You then get a blue YOU dot on the maps, the distance and direction to every stop, a Near me list of the ten closest waypoints, and a pop-up when you reach one — within about 120 m of a green HIGH pin, 300 m of a yellow MEDIUM and 800 m of a red LOW area. The app has to be open on screen, and it works when opened from its web address (https://…). Your location never leaves your phone — nothing is sent or stored anywhere. Tap Turn off to stop.

Using the map buttons

The Google Maps button on every stop opens a pin on the exact waypoint — not directions from where you are — so you can see the spot first and ask for directions when you want them. On the Tour tab each day also has a big Google Maps route button that loads the whole day's stops, in order, as one route. Tap ✓ on a stop to mark it visited — the tick is remembered on this device only. Everything you write or tick stays on your phone: there are no accounts and no tracking. On an iPhone, adding the guide to the Home Screen keeps your ticks and notes safe.

Where the sources disagree

Every stop in this guide was researched against official histories, war-graves and memorial records, the museums' own websites and other sources, and the main claims were checked again. Where sources could not agree, or a story is disputed, the text says so — look for Where the sources disagree on a stop. The main cases:

  • How many Soviet dead?. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people, soldiers and civilians, according to the figure published in 1990 from demographic calculations; Stalin had admitted 7 million, Khrushchev 20 million. For military deaths, the Russian General Staff study led by G. F. Krivosheev gives about 8.7 million, including prisoners who died in captivity. Some Russian and Western researchers argue that this is too low and that military dead may have exceeded 11 million. Civilian deaths are harder still to count, because the borders of 1941 and the population of the occupied lands are themselves uncertain.
  • The halt before Dunkirk. On 24 May 1940 Hitler confirmed a halt of the panzers short of Dunkirk, which gave the Allies time to organise the perimeter and the evacuation. Why is still argued. The halt was proposed by Rundstedt, commanding Army Group A, to rest and repair his tanks for the battle still to come in the south and to avoid the canals and marshes round Dunkirk; Göring promised that the Luftwaffe could finish the job. The idea that Hitler let the British go to make peace easier comes mainly from later claims and is doubted by most historians.
  • How big was Prokhorovka?. Soviet histories described Prokhorovka on 12 July 1943 as the greatest tank battle in history, with some 1,500 tanks and a German armoured force smashed. Research in German and Soviet archives since the 1990s — by Karl-Heinz Frieser, Valeriy Zamulin, David Glantz and others — shows roughly 600 Soviet tanks and self-propelled guns against fewer than 300 German. The Soviets lost around 300–400 tanks that day; German permanent losses were small, perhaps only a handful, though many more were damaged. The Soviet attack nevertheless stopped the SS Panzer Corps, and the offensive was called off.
  • The Dresden death toll. For decades, figures of 135,000, 200,000 or even more were quoted for the dead of the February 1945 raids on Dresden. They began with Nazi propaganda, which added a nought to a police report, and were spread after the war, notably by David Irving on the basis of a forged document. A historians' commission set up by the city reported in 2010 that between 18,000 and 25,000 people died. The moral argument over the raid — military necessity or terror bombing — continues separately from the numbers.
  • Katyn. When Germany announced the discovery of the Katyn graves in April 1943, the Soviet Union blamed the Germans, broke off relations with the Polish government in London when it asked for a Red Cross inquiry, and in 1944 produced its own commission report. The Soviets even raised Katyn at the Nuremberg trials, where the charge was quietly dropped. Western governments, needing Stalin, said little. Only in 1990 did the Soviet Union admit that the NKVD had carried out the killings; some Russian investigation files remain closed, and the full list of victims from Belarus has never been published.
  • Why did the Red Army stop at Warsaw?. When the Home Army rose in August 1944, the Red Army stood a few kilometres from Warsaw and then halted. One view stresses military reasons: the Soviet armies were exhausted after advancing hundreds of kilometres in Bagration, and German panzer divisions had just defeated their spearhead north-east of the city. The other stresses Stalin's politics: he wanted no independent Polish authority in the capital, and for weeks refused Allied supply aircraft the use of Soviet airfields. Most historians accept that both played a part; they disagree on the balance.
  • Who lost at Arnhem?. Montgomery called Market Garden '90 per cent successful'; others see it as an avoidable failure. Blame has been laid on the plan's single road, on intelligence warnings about SS panzer units near Arnhem that were discounted, on drop zones 10–13 km from the bridge, on radios that did not work, on the delay at Nijmegen and on the slow advance of XXX Corps. Major-General Sosabowski of the Polish Parachute Brigade, who had warned against the plan, was removed from command afterwards — a decision widely seen today as unjust.
  • Numbers murdered in the camps. Early post-war figures for individual camps were often far too high: a Soviet commission put the dead of Auschwitz at 4 million, which stood on the memorial until 1990, and Majdanek's at 1.5 million. Research in the camp records, transport lists and population data has since produced lower, better-founded figures — about 1.1 million for Auschwitz (Franciszek Piper), about 78,000 for Majdanek (Tomasz Kranz). Treblinka estimates range from about 800,000 to 925,000. These revisions do not change the total of about six million Jews murdered, which rests on separate population studies.
  • Myths of 'the Few'. Some 2,900 aircrew of Fighter Command took part in the Battle of Britain, and about 544 were killed. They were not only British: about one in five came from elsewhere, including Poles, Czechs, New Zealanders, Canadians and others, and the Polish No. 303 Squadron had the best record of any. Nor were they hopelessly outnumbered in fighters. Their success owed much to radar and the control system, to Hurricanes as much as Spitfires, and to German errors. Some historians argue that the Royal Navy, rather than Fighter Command alone, was the real barrier to invasion.
  • Positions and battle maps. Every pin carries an accuracy label. The battle maps are schematic: front lines, arrows and unit positions are drawn by hand from historical maps and are approximate.

How many days?
